issue_context.title: Non LoadBalancer Types can set Status.Loadbalancer.Ingress
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

I can set the Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress in Services that are not Type LoadBalancer

**What you expected to happen**:

The apiserver should reject the Status update

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1. kind create cluster
2. wget https://gist.githubusercontent.com/aojea/94e20cda0f4e4de16fe8e35afc678732/raw/a18045d651232c6d20a790503d1eba88c89cc5bc/lb_ingress.py
3. sudo pip install kubernetes
4. kubectl run test --image httpd --port 80
5. kubectl expose pod test
6. python lb_ingress.py default test 1.1.1.1
7. kubectl get services test -o yaml

```
  selfLink: /api/v1/namespaces/default/services/test
  uid: b799e259-c995-4a8a-aed9-df9bfa458f6f
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.97.81.50
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    run: test
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
status:
  loadBalancer:
    ingress:
    - ip: 1.1.1.1
```
comments:
Thanks Andres and Tim for the explanation, for the record, discussion is here
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/96726#discussion_r527366498

review_comments: I know of some use-cases where it's useful to set `service.Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress` without the type being `LoadBalancer`. It's maybe far fetched, but `status.loadbalancer.ingress.ip` is useful for binding Services to arbitrary VIPs where you can't use ClusterIP since it must be in the service range and you can't use ExternalIPs cause internal traffic is dropped
I'd also consider this a breaking change since I'm sure there's a non-trivial amount of users setting service status without the type being load balancer.

On one hand, normal users should NOT have access to service Status.  What you are describing sounds...awful.

On the other hand, I have been trying to be even-handed about saying "no, that's a breaking change", even when I like the change.  So I think Andrew's right - we can't actually do this.  We can log and even throw an event when we observe this, but we can't break it.  There's not even a protocol for doing this over some extended period of time.  The rule is simply "we don't break the API" (on purpose, at least).

:(

> "we don't break the API" (on purpose, at least).

yeah, that was I was wondering too, this seems to be like this since forever :shrug: 

> ExternalIPs cause internal traffic is dropped

That is another thing I stumbled on recently, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/95785#issuecomment-722928906
is it on purpose or an implementation detail? 
I can't see a reason to not allow internal traffic to ExternalIPs
